paragraphs: The remaining powers that the Convention's plan gives the Senate in a distinct capacity are two: its share with the executive in appointments to office, and its judicial character as a court for trying impeachments. In the business of appointments the executive will be the principal agent, so the provisions on that subject are best discussed when we examine that department. We will therefore conclude this head with a look at the judicial character of the Senate.

A well-constituted court for trying impeachments is as hard to obtain as it is to be desired, in a government that is wholly elective. The matters within its jurisdiction are those offenses that come from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust. They are of a kind that may with particular propriety be called POLITICAL, since they relate chiefly to injuries done directly to society itself. For this reason their prosecution will seldom fail to stir the passions of the whole community and to divide it into parties more or less friendly or hostile to the accused. In many cases it will attach itself to existing factions and will enlist all their animosities, biases, influence and interest on one side or the other. In such cases there will always be the greatest danger that the decision will be governed more by the relative strength of the parties than by the real proofs of innocence or guilt.

The delicacy and magnitude of a trust that so deeply concerns the political reputation and existence of every man engaged in the administration of public affairs speak for themselves. The difficulty of placing it rightly, in a government resting entirely on periodic elections, will be as readily seen when we consider this: the most conspicuous figures in such a government will, for that very reason, too often be the leaders or the tools of the most cunning or the most numerous faction. For this reason they can hardly be expected to have the neutrality required toward those whose conduct may be under scrutiny.

The Convention, it appears, judged the Senate the fittest keeper of this important trust. Those who can best see the inherent difficulty of the matter will be the slowest to condemn that opinion, and the most inclined to give due weight to the arguments that may be supposed to have produced it.

What, it may be asked, is the true spirit of the institution itself? Is it not designed as a method of NATIONAL INQUEST into the conduct of public men? If that is its design, who can be so proper to act as inquisitors for the nation as the representatives of the nation themselves? It is not disputed that the power to begin the inquiry, or in other words to bring the impeachment, ought to be placed in the hands of one branch of the legislative body. Will not the reasons that show the propriety of this arrangement argue strongly for admitting the other branch of that body to a share in the inquiry? The model from which the idea of this institution was borrowed pointed out that course to the Convention. In Great Britain it is the province of the House of Commons to bring the impeachment and of the House of Lords to decide it. Several of the State constitutions have followed the example. Both the latter and the former seem to have regarded impeachment as a bridle in the hands of the legislative body upon the executive servants of the government. Is not this the true light in which it ought to be regarded?

Where else but in the Senate could a court have been found that is sufficiently dignified or sufficiently independent? What other body would be likely to feel CONFIDENCE ENOUGH IN ITS OWN SITUATION to keep, unawed and uninfluenced, the necessary impartiality between an INDIVIDUAL accused and the REPRESENTATIVES OF THE PEOPLE, HIS ACCUSERS?

Could the Supreme Court have been relied on to meet this description? It is much to be doubted whether the members of that court would at all times have so eminent a portion of fortitude as so difficult a task would demand. It is still more doubtful whether they would have the degree of credit and authority that might on certain occasions be indispensable for reconciling the people to a decision that happened to clash with an accusation brought by their immediate representatives. A deficiency in the first would be fatal to the accused; in the second, dangerous to public tranquillity. The risk in both respects could be avoided, if at all, only by making that court more numerous than would be consistent with reasonable attention to economy. The nature of the proceeding equally requires a numerous court for trying impeachments. This proceeding can never be tied down by such strict rules, either in how the prosecutors define the offense or in how the judges construe it, as in ordinary cases serve to limit the discretion of courts in favor of personal security. There will be no jury to stand between the judges who are to pronounce the sentence of the law and the party who is to receive or suffer it. The awesome discretion that a court of impeachments must necessarily have, to doom to honor or to infamy the most trusted and most distinguished characters in the community, forbids committing the trust to a small number of persons.

These considerations alone seem enough to justify the conclusion that the Supreme Court would have been an improper substitute for the Senate as a court of impeachments. There is a further consideration that will do much to strengthen this conclusion. It is this: the punishment that may follow conviction on impeachment is not to end the offender's chastisement. After being sentenced to a perpetual banishment from the esteem and confidence, and the honors and pay, of his country, he will still be liable to prosecution and punishment in the ordinary course of law. Would it be proper that the persons who had disposed of his reputation and his most valuable rights as a citizen in one trial should, in another trial for the same offense, also dispose of his life and his fortune? Would there not be the greatest reason to fear that error in the first sentence would be the parent of error in the second? That the strong bias of one decision would be apt to overrule the influence of any new lights that might be brought to change the complexion of another decision? Those who know anything of human nature will not hesitate to answer these questions in the affirmative. They will have no trouble seeing that by making the same persons judges in both cases, those who happened to be the objects of prosecution would be largely deprived of the double security a double trial was meant to give them. The loss of life and estate would often be virtually included in a sentence that, in its terms, meant nothing more than dismissal from a present office and disqualification for a future one. It may be said that bringing in a jury in the second case would remove the danger. But juries are often influenced by the opinions of judges. They are sometimes induced to return special verdicts, which refer the main question to the decision of the court. Who would be willing to stake his life and his estate on the verdict of a jury acting under the auspices of judges who had already decided he was guilty?

Would it have improved the plan to unite the Supreme Court with the Senate in forming the court of impeachments? This union would certainly have had several advantages. But would they not have been outweighed by the serious disadvantage already stated, which arises from the same judges' taking part in the double prosecution to which the offender would be liable? To a certain extent the benefits of that union will be obtained by making the chief justice of the Supreme Court the president of the court of impeachments, as the Convention's plan proposes. At the same time the problems of fully merging the former into the latter will be substantially avoided. This was perhaps the prudent middle course. I refrain from remarking on the additional pretext for clamor against the judiciary that so considerable an increase of its authority would have given.

Would it have been desirable to compose the court for the trial of impeachments of persons wholly distinct from the other departments of the government? There are weighty arguments both against and in favor of such a plan. To some minds it will not seem a trivial objection that it would tend to increase the complexity of the political machine and to add a new spring to the government, the usefulness of which would at best be questionable. But there is an objection that no one will think unworthy of attention: a court formed on such a plan would either entail heavy expense or might in practice be subject to a variety of mishaps and problems. It must consist either of permanent officers, stationed at the seat of government and therefore entitled to fixed and regular salaries, or of certain officers of the State governments, to be called on whenever an impeachment was actually pending. It will not be easy to imagine any third method, materially different, that could reasonably be proposed. As the court ought to be numerous, for reasons already given, the first scheme will be condemned by every man who can compare the extent of the public needs with the means of meeting them. The second will be adopted only with caution by those who seriously consider several things: the difficulty of gathering men scattered over the whole Union; the injury to the innocent from the long delay in deciding the charges that might be brought against them; the advantage to the guilty from the opportunities that delay would give for intrigue and corruption; and in some cases the damage to the State from the prolonged inaction of men whose firm and faithful performance of their duty might have exposed them to the persecution of an intemperate or scheming majority in the House of Representatives. This last supposition may seem harsh, and might not often be borne out, yet it should not be forgotten that the demon of faction will at certain seasons extend his scepter over all numerous bodies of men.

But suppose one or the other of the substitutes we have examined, or some other that might be devised, were thought preferable in this respect to the plan reported by the Convention. It would not follow that the Constitution ought for that reason to be rejected. If mankind were to resolve to agree on no institution of government until every part of it had been adjusted to the most exact standard of perfection, society would soon become a general scene of anarchy and the world a desert. Where is the standard of perfection to be found? Who will undertake to bring the clashing opinions of a whole community to the same judgment of it, and to persuade one conceited projector to give up his INFALLIBLE criterion for the FALLIBLE criterion of his more CONCEITED neighbor? To serve the purpose of the adversaries of the Constitution, they ought to prove, not merely that particular provisions in it are not the best that could have been imagined, but that the plan on the whole is bad and destructive.
